analysis.one_liner: Lets California and other states enforce their own stricter greenhouse gas limits on cars and light trucks.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In December 2007, the head of the EPA denied California's request to enforce its own stricter limits on greenhouse gases from cars and light trucks — the first outright denial of such a request in decades, according to the bill's own findings. This bill would have changed the Clean Air Act so that California's request was approved by law, letting California and the dozen-plus states that follow its standards immediately require cleaner vehicles without waiting for years of litigation. The bill cleared the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and was placed on the Senate's waiting list for floor action, but no vote ever came.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of California and the 14 states that had adopted or were adopting the California standards — together representing more than half the U.S. population — who would get vehicles that emit less carbon dioxide and other pollutants. The bill's findings cite California Air Resources Board analysis that the California standards would cut carbon dioxide emissions in California roughly twice as much by 2020 as the new federal fuel-economy program, and more than 80 percent more nationally [S4]. State governments would also gain certainty and avoid years of litigation against the federal government to defend their rules [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Half the U.S. population in California-standard states

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Clean Air Act to deem California's December 2005 waiver request approved, letting the state enforce its greenhouse gas rules for cars and light trucks immediately instead of suing the federal government for several years

Fourteen other states had adopted or were adopting the California standards and four more were moving toward them — together covering more than half the U.S. population — so approval would extend stricter vehicle standards to most of the country

California's standards would cut carbon dioxide emissions about twice as much in California, and more than 80 percent more nationally, as the federal fuel-economy program alone, according to California Air Resources Board analysis cited in the bill

The bill documents that EPA had granted more than 50 prior California waiver requests over four decades and had never flatly denied one, and that over 99.9 percent of roughly 98,000 public comments on the docket supported granting this one

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would have to build and sell vehicles meeting stricter emissions standards in California-standard states covering more than half the country, raising engineering and compliance costs that are typically passed partly to new-car buyers. Refiners and sellers of gasoline would face somewhat lower demand as vehicles became more efficient. The committee's Republicans filed formal minority views opposing the bill [S6].
analysis.who_pays_short: Automakers, oil refiners, some new-car buyers

drawbacks.text: Automakers and their allies argued that a national fuel-economy law enacted in December 2007 (the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007) was already reducing emissions and that a separate California standard would create a 'confusing patchwork' of state rules; the bill's findings rebut the patchwork point by noting the two-standard system has existed for 30 years, but the compliance-cost concern for manufacturers and consumers is real
Stricter emissions requirements raise the engineering cost of new vehicles, some of which lands on new-car buyers; the bill offers no offsetting compensation to manufacturers

The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee's Republicans filed formal minority views against the bill when it was reported out, signaling substantial Republican opposition even before the floor stage

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — faster and deeper cuts in vehicle greenhouse gas emissions across states holding more than half the U.S. population, with near-unanimous public support on the record — is large and the main cost, higher compliance costs for automakers that partly pass through to car buyers, is the ordinary cost of emissions regulation that the auto industry has absorbed for decades under California's 40-year-old, stricter-than-federal standards. The bill is narrow and targeted: it does not set new national policy, it simply restores a state-federal arrangement that had worked for 40 years. An honest accounting favors the bill, though automakers' cost objections were made in good faith and the 2007 federal fuel-economy law does overlap with what California requires.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved it and it was placed on the Senate's list of bills waiting for floor action, but Senate leaders never brought it to a vote and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 24, 2008 by Senator Boxer with 27 cosponsors including three Republicans, in direct response to EPA Administrator Stephen Johnson's December 19, 2007 denial of California's waiver request — the first outright denial of a California vehicle-standards waiver in the Clean Air Act's history, after more than 50 prior grants

On May 21, 2008 the Environment and Public Works Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on June 27, 2008 it was reported by Senator Boxer with a written report and minority views filed by committee Republicans
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 861), the waiting list for floor action, on June 27, 2008
No further action was ever taken; the Senate never voted on the bill, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009

Fourteen states had adopted or were adopting California's standards and four more were moving toward them, covering more than half the U.S. population, all of whom were left waiting on federal action or litigation

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers benefited first: they did not have to meet the stricter California standards in half the country during 2008, and the states were left to litigate rather than regulate. The Bush EPA's denial also stood. The following year, under a new administration, the EPA granted the California waiver, so the policy eventually happened — but this Congress's inaction delayed it by about a year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers and the outgoing administration's EPA

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, reported it favorably out of the Environment and Public Works Committee and placed it on the Senate calendar

for.name: 27 Senate cosponsors (22 Democrats, 1 Independent Democrat, 1 Independent, 3 Republicans)
for.role: Cosponsors of S. 2555, including Sens. Obama, Clinton, Biden, Collins, Snowe, and Warner
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing from states representing more than half the U.S. population

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, where it sat until the Congress expired

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Republicans
against.role: Minority members of the reporting committee
against.what_they_did: Filed formal minority views against the bill when it was reported out of committee on June 27, 2008

against.name: EPA Administrator Stephen Johnson
against.what_they_did: Denied California's waiver request on December 19, 2007 — the action the bill was written to overturn — over the documented opposition of the auto industry

against.name: Automakers
against.what_they_did: Opposed California's greenhouse gas standards and lobbied against the waiver, arguing the new federal fuel-economy law made state standards unnecessary and a patchwork of rules costly

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 22 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 3 Republicans — but committee Republicans filed minority views against the bill, and no floor vote occurred that would show how the parties lined up.

industries.note: The bill would require them to meet California's stricter greenhouse gas standards in states covering more than half the U.S. population, raising vehicle engineering and compliance costs. Their preference for the weaker federal-only standard comes directly at the cost of the emission reductions the bill would deliver to the public.

More efficient, lower-emitting vehicles cut gasoline consumption, shrinking fuel sales. The industry's interest in weaker vehicle standards runs against the public's interest in lower emissions and lower fuel bills.

The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Sciences on California's role as 'a proving ground for new emissions-control technologies'; a guaranteed large market for cleaner vehicles would expand demand for them, and the resulting innovation benefits the whole country.
